The Wedge-pulling Monkey

In a city, a merchant was building a temple. Workers went to the city for lunch at noon.

A troop of monkeys found the half-built temple. One monkey, curious, pulled a wedge from a beam. The beam fell, and the monkey was hurt.

The king, who had been warned about the monkey's misbehavior, was angry. He sent his counselor's son, Victor, to find the monkey who had pulled the wedge.

Victor searched the forest and found the monkey. He asked the monkey why he had pulled the wedge. The monkey replied, "I was curious. I wanted to know what the wedge was for."

Victor said, "You should not have pulled the wedge. It was a foolish act." The monkey replied, "I did not know it would cause harm."

Victor continued, "You must learn to think before acting. If you had thought, you would not have pulled the wedge." The monkey looked down, ashamed.

The king, impressed with Victor's words, decided to make him his new counselor. Victor was happy and proud to serve the king.

The Lion and the Carpenter

In a forest, a carpenter named Trust-god lived with his wife. They spent their days cutting logs. A lion named Spotless, with a jackal and a crow as his friends, lived in the same forest.

One day, the lion met the carpenter. The carpenter, seeing the lion, approached him calmly and said, "Come, friend! I'll share my lunch with you." The lion, being carnivorous, said he didn't eat rice, but he'd try the carpenter's food. The carpenter fed him sweets and treats, and the lion was pleased.

To show his gratitude, the lion promised to let the carpenter pass through the forest safely. The carpenter asked the lion to come alone each day, but the lion's friends, the jackal and the crow, were jealous. They begged the lion to take them to the carpenter's house, where they could eat his food.

The lion told them he visited a friend who fed him delicious food, but he didn't want to take them. The jackal and the crow decided to kill the carpenter and take his food for themselves. The lion, however, felt guilty and said he'd get some food for them.

The three friends set out to find the carpenter. When they arrived, the carpenter and his wife were already in a tree. The lion explained that he was his friend, but the carpenter refused to come down, saying, "I don't trust your friends, and I'm not comfortable with them around."

The lion realized that the carpenter was right and that his friends were troublemakers. He decided to stay away from them and find a better way to get food. From then on, the lion visited the carpenter alone, and they became good friends.

Moral: A person's character can be judged by the company they keep.

The Plover Who Fought the Ocean

 

A plover and his wife lived by the sea. They were called Sprawl and Constance.

The sea had many fish, crocodiles, and turtles. Constance was pregnant and wanted to lay her eggs safely.

Sprawl said, "Don't worry, this is our home. The ocean is far away." Constance said, "But the ocean is close. Its waves might hurt my babies."

Sprawl said, "The ocean won't hurt me. I'm a strong plover." He started talking loudly and said, "Who dares to fight a snake? Who touches a hot fire?"

Constance laughed and said, "You talk big, but you're not brave. You're just a loud talker." She said, "To know yourself is hard. You should think before acting."

Constance told a story about a turtle who listened to his friends. He was happy and safe. Sprawl asked, "How was that?" Constance said, "It's wise to listen to friends."

Constance laid her eggs in a safe place. Sprawl was proud of himself, but he was wrong. The ocean's waves came and went, but they didn't hurt the plover's home.

Moral: Listen to others and think before acting.

The Plover Who Fought the Ocean

 

Sprawl and his wife Constance lived by the sea, where fish, crocodiles, and turtles thrived. Constance was pregnant and needed a safe place to lay her eggs. "Find a spot for me," she said to Sprawl. "Why worry?" he replied, "our home is perfect. The ocean can't harm us."

But Constance wasn't convinced. "What if the ocean's tide reaches us and swallows our babies?" she asked. Sprawl chuckled and began to boast about his bravery. "I'm not afraid of the ocean! Who dares to challenge me?" he said. But his wife wasn't impressed.

Constance laughed at Sprawl's boasts and said, "You're just a show-off! You think you're brave, but you don't know your own strength and weakness. It's hard to know yourself, but it's essential to success." She reminded him of a wise saying: "Accurate self-critics are secure in times of trouble."

Sprawl was taken aback. His wife was right – he had been foolish to boast about his bravery. Constance continued, "And don't forget, it's wise to listen to friendly advice. Even a turtle learns from his friends." Sprawl looked at his wife with newfound respect, realizing he had been foolish to underestimate the ocean's power.

The Girl Who Married a Snake

In a faraway city, a Brahman named Godly lived. He and his wife had no children.

One day, Godly said, "Don't worry, my dear. I had a special dream. We will have a very special son."

The wife was happy. She waited and waited. Then she had a baby. But when she saw him, she was shocked. He was a snake!

The neighbors said, "Throw him away!" But the wife loved him. She took care of him, fed him milk and butter.

As the snake grew, the wife loved him more and more. She said, "I want a marriage festival for my boy!"

Godly said, "Who would give their daughter to a snake?" But he loved his wife, so he went on a long journey to find a wife for the snake.

He traveled to a faraway city called Kutkuta City. He met a kind host who gave him food and shelter.

The next morning, Godly said, "I'm looking for a wife for my son." His host said, "I have a beautiful daughter. Take her!"

Godly took the girl to his home. But when people saw her, they said, "A snake? She's too beautiful for him!"

The girl's relatives said, "Take her away from the snake!" But the girl said, "No! I will marry him!"

She told them about a wise person named Blossom. Blossom had a very hard life, but she never gave up. The girl said, "I will be like Blossom. I will be happy with my snake husband."

Moral: Be brave and happy with what you have.

The Girl Who Married a Snake

In a kingdom called Palace City, a Brahman named Godly lived with his wife. She was childless and often wept at the sight of her neighbors' children.

One day, Godly said to his wife, "Don't be sad. Remember when I offered a sacrifice for a child? An invisible voice said I'd have a son who would surpass everyone in beauty, character, and charm."

The wife's heart swelled with joy. "I hope these promises come true," she said. Soon, she gave birth to a snake. Her friends advised her to throw it away, but she took care of it like a baby.

She bathed the snake, fed it milk and butter, and kept it in a clean box. Before long, the snake grew up. The Brahman's wife was so proud of her son.

At a neighbor's son's wedding, the Brahman's wife said to her husband, "Why don't you arrange a wedding for our son?" Godly replied, "Who would give their daughter to a snake? I'd have to go to the underworld and beg Vasuki, the serpent-king."

Godly was disturbed by his wife's sad face, so he packed his bags and traveled to a distant land called Kutkuta City. He stayed with a kinsman who treated him kindly.

The next morning, Godly's host asked, "What brought you here?" Godly replied, "I'm searching for a bride for my son." His host said, "I have a beautiful daughter. Take her for your son."

The Brahman took the girl and her attendants back home. When the people saw her, they were amazed by her beauty. They said, "How can we give such a wonderful girl to a snake?" The girl's relatives were worried, but she said, "I'll marry the snake, and that's final."

When they asked her why, she said, "My father's promise was true. I'll marry the snake, and it's not up for discussion." When they asked about the girl named Blossom, she told them the story of a girl who was once married to a snake.

Moral: True promises and fate are unchangeable, and we must accept what is destined.

Right-Mind and Wrong-Mind

In a bustling city, two friends, Right-Mind and Wrong-Mind, lived with their merchant fathers. They decided to travel to a distant land to earn money and make their families proud.

As they wandered, Right-Mind stumbled upon a hidden pot containing a thousand dinars, left behind by a wise holy man. He shared the news with Wrong-Mind, and they agreed to return home together.

Upon their return, Right-Mind suggested they split the treasure equally, but Wrong-Mind proposed a clever plan. He convinced Right-Mind to divide the money into smaller portions, burying the rest and promising to share the remaining wealth.

Right-Mind, trusting his friend, agreed to the plan. Wrong-Mind, however, had no intention of sharing. He spent his share recklessly, and soon he needed more. He convinced Right-Mind to divide the remaining treasure, and eventually, he convinced himself that it was okay to steal the rest.

When Right-Mind discovered the theft, Wrong-Mind accused him of stealing the treasure. The two friends took their dispute to court, where magistrates decided to conduct an ordeal to determine the guilty party.

Wrong-Mind claimed to have a witness, the goddess of the forest, who would reveal the truth. The magistrates agreed, and Wrong-Mind's father was asked to be a witness. However, Right-Mind's father suspected foul play and warned his son about the dangers of clever schemes.

Moral: Clever plans often hide a hidden trap, and trusting someone who is not trustworthy can lead to trouble.

Mother Shandilee's Bargain

A Brahman and his wife lived in a town.

The Brahman was a kind man. He gave shelter to guests.

One rainy day, I asked for shelter. He gave it to me.

I lived with them, doing good deeds.

One day, I woke up early. I heard the Brahman and his wife talking.

The Brahman said, "Tomorrow is the winter solstice. I will go to another village to collect donations."

His wife said, "Who will give food to a poor Brahman like you? You should be ashamed."

The Brahman was scared. He said, "My dear, don't say that. Even if you have little, give something to those in need."

The Brahman told a story. "A cloud gives only water, but the world treats it with respect. The sun gives much, but no one likes it."

The Brahman's wife asked, "How was that?" The Brahman said, "It means that even a little help is good when given at the right time."

Moral: Even a small gift can bring great happiness.

Mother Shandilee's Bargain

 

A Brahman named Shandilee came to live with a family in a town for the rainy season. He helped with household chores and did his daily prayers.

One morning, Shandilee overheard his host and his wife talking about the winter solstice. The Brahman said, "My dear, it's a great time for donations. We should feed a poor Brahman." But his wife snapped back, "Who would give to a poor Brahman like you? You're not even ashamed?"

Shandilee's wife was bitter about their poverty. She said, "I've never had a thing since I married you. We've never eaten fancy food or even seen a gem or a ring." The Brahman was taken aback and stuttered, "My dear, you shouldn't say that. Even the poor should give what they can to those in need."

Shandilee reminded his wife about the importance of giving. "Even a small gift can make a big difference. The cloud gives only water, but the whole world treats it with respect. We should give what we can, when we can." He also quoted a wise saying, "A little helps in time of need, but excessive greed leads to trouble."

The wife asked, "What's that supposed to mean?" Shandilee explained that giving with a kind heart and at the right time brings great rewards. His wife was still skeptical, but Shandilee's words stayed with her.

Moral: Even the smallest act of kindness can bring great rewards when done with a generous heart.

Soft, the Weaver

In a town, a weaver named Soft lived. He made beautiful clothes. But he never had enough money.

His wife said, "Don't move. You'll be okay here."

Soft said, "No, I'll go to Growing City. I'll earn more money."

He went to Growing City and stayed three years. He earned 300 gold-pieces and started home.

In a forest, he climbed a banyan tree to sleep. He saw two men arguing.

One said, "You gave Soft 300 gold-pieces. Why did you do that?"

The other said, "I give rewards to those who work hard. It's not my problem."

Soft woke up and found his bag empty. He thought, "Oh no! I worked hard for nothing."

He went back to Growing City and earned 500 gold-pieces in one year. He started home again.

In the forest, he saw the same two men arguing again.

One said, "You gave Soft 500 gold-pieces. He doesn't get anything beyond food and clothes."

The other said, "I give rewards to those who work hard. It's not my problem."

Soft woke up again and found his bag empty. He thought, "I'll just hang myself from this tree."

But a figure appeared in the sky and said, "Don't be so rash, Soft. I'm the one who takes your money. You can go home. Ask for what you want."

Soft said, "Give me plenty of money."

The figure said, "What will you do with money if you can't enjoy it or give it away? You can only use it for food and clothes."

Soft said, "I still want it. It will make me look important."

The figure asked, "How is that?"

Soft told the story of how people with money are respected, even if they are not good-looking.

Moral: What is meant to be yours will come to you, no matter where you go.

Soft, the Weaver

In a small town, Soft, a skilled weaver, made beautiful garments for princes. Despite his hard work, he struggled to earn more than just enough food and clothes for himself and his wife. He saw other weavers making coarse fabrics and earning a lot of money, which made him think of moving to a new city.

His wife, wise and understanding, tried to persuade him to stay. She believed that fate decided how much wealth a person would have, and that traveling wouldn't change their fortunes. She shared her thoughts with him, but Soft was determined to leave.

Soft moved to Growing City, where he worked hard and eventually saved three hundred gold-pieces. On his way back home, he stopped in a forest to rest. As he slept, he had a strange dream. In the dream, two figures, Doer and Deed, argued about Soft's wealth. Doer, who seemed to be in charge, said that Soft deserved the money he earned. Deed, on the other hand, claimed that he was responsible for giving Soft the money.

Soft woke up, feeling puzzled and worried. He searched his bag and found it empty. He thought, "Oh no! All my hard work for nothing!" He decided to return to Growing City, where he earned even more money, this time five hundred gold-pieces, in just one year.

On his way back, he stopped at the same banyan tree and had another strange dream. The two figures reappeared, arguing about Soft's new wealth. This time, Doer defended Soft's right to the money. Soft woke up again, feeling frustrated and hopeless. He thought, "What's the point of earning money if I'll just lose it?" He decided to hang himself from the banyan tree.

Just as he was about to let himself drop, a figure appeared in the sky. It was the one responsible for taking Soft's money. The figure told Soft to go home and not be so quick to give up. Soft asked for plenty of money, but the figure explained that he wouldn't be able to enjoy it or give it away. Soft replied, "Even if I can't use it, I want it for the sake of having it."

The figure was impressed with Soft's determination and decided to grant his wish. Soft returned home, where he and his wife lived happily ever after.

Moral: The true value of wealth lies not in its accumulation, but in the ability to enjoy and share it with others.

How the Birds Picked a King

The birds of the forest gathered together.

They were swans, cranes, nightingales, and many more.

They said, "We need a king. But Garuda is busy with his god. He doesn't help us when we need him."

The birds looked around and saw the owl.

"Let's make the owl our king," they said.

They prepared a throne and brought water from holy streams.

They gave the owl a special dress and made him sit on the throne.

Just then, a crow came in. He was very clever.

The birds said, "Let's ask the crow what he thinks."

The crow said, "No, no! You can't make the owl king. He's ugly and mean. He's not a good choice."

The birds asked the crow why not.

The crow said, "We already have a good king, Garuda. Why do we need another one?"

The birds thought about what the crow said.

They decided to ask the owl to be their king.

The owl was very happy.

Moral: It's not wise to have two leaders, when one is good enough.

How the Birds Picked a King

The birds of different species gathered for a consultation.

There were swans, cranes, nightingales, peacocks, plovers, owls, doves, pigeons, partridges, bluejays, vultures, skylarks, demoiselles, cuckoos, and woodpeckers. They complained about their current king, Garuda, who ignored their problems and didn't defend them when needed.

The birds decided to choose a new king, and since the owl looked wise, they suggested him for the job. They prepared a grand ceremony, filling the air with the scent of holy streams, flowers, and incense.

As the owl waited for the anointing, a crow suddenly appeared, thinking, "What's all this fuss about?" The birds welcomed the crow, thinking he was the wisest of birds, and asked for his opinion.

The crow, however, laughed and said, "You're making a huge mistake! Why choose a blind owl when you have such beautiful and talented birds as yourselves? The owl is ugly, fierce, and mean-spirited. You'll fail with him as your king."

The crow reminded them that they already had a good king, Garuda, and that having two kings would be chaotic. He quoted proverbs to emphasize his point, saying that a single, strong king was better than multiple weak ones.

The birds looked at each other, unsure of what to do.

How the Rabbit Fooled the Elephant

In a forest lived an elephant-king named Four-Tusk, who protected his herd. A severe drought struck, and the elephants begged for a solution. Four-Tusk sent eight groups to search for water in different directions.

One group discovered the Lake of the Moon, a beautiful lake with swans, herons, and other water creatures. The lake was surrounded by flowering trees and had a gentle slope, perfect for elephants to bathe. However, the elephants didn't notice the rabbits living on the banks.

The rabbits, who had lost many of their family members, held an emergency meeting. They asked Victory, a wise rabbit, to come up with a plan to prevent the elephants from returning. Victory promised to stop the elephants and said he had received a special gift from his guardian angel.

The rabbit-king, Block-Snout, trusted Victory and sent him to meet the elephant-king. Victory climbed a rock-pile and introduced himself as an envoy from the Moon. The elephant-king, Four-Tusk, was impressed by Victory's confidence and asked him to state his business.

Victory explained that as an envoy, he was protected by the laws of kings. He told Four-Tusk that he had sinned against the Moon by killing the rabbits who were under its protection. Four-Tusk felt guilty and asked Victory to show him the way to win the Moon's forgiveness.

Victory led Four-Tusk to the Lake of the Moon at night and showed him the reflection of the Moon in the water. Four-Tusk was amazed by the beauty of the Moon and its companions. He felt ashamed and decided to purify himself by washing his trunk in the lake.

However, Victory was shocked to see Four-Tusk touch the water, which he knew would anger the Moon even more. Four-Tusk realized his mistake and bowed his head in deep obeisance, asking for forgiveness.

Moral: Pretending to be something you're not can lead to trouble, and honesty is always the best policy.

The Cave That Talked

There was a hungry lion named Rough-Claw. He had no food to eat. He was very thirsty.

Rough-Claw found a big cave in a mountain. He went inside to rest. The cave belonged to a jackal named Curd-Face. Curd-Face came to the cave door and sang: "Hello! Cave ahoy!"

Rough-Claw thought: "This cave always calls out a greeting. But today, it's silent. I will call out a greeting." Rough-Claw roared loudly.

The cave's echo was very loud. It scared other animals far away. Curd-Face ran away, laughing.

Curd-Face met a friend named Red-Eye. Red-Eye said: "I know why you ran away. You were scared of the lion." Curd-Face said: "Yes, I was scared."

Red-Eye met another friend named Live-Strong. Live-Strong said: "I know why you ran away. You were scared of the lion." Red-Eye said: "No, I was scared because I knew the lion was hungry."

Live-Strong thought: "I can use the lion to get rid of my enemies. I will make a plan." Live-Strong and Red-Eye came up with a plan to trick the lion.

The lion, Curd-Face, and the owls were all fooled. They thought the lion was going to be their friend. But Live-Strong had a different plan. He wanted to get rid of them.

Moral: Don't trust your enemies, and be careful who you trust.

The Frogs That Rode Snakeback

There was once a lazy black snake named Slow-Poison who lived near a pond. He thought to himself, "How can I get along without using too much energy?" He decided to visit the pond and pretend to be sad.

A curious frog approached him and asked, "Uncle, why aren't you catching food like usual?" Slow-Poison explained that he was cursed by a Brahman's son. He said, "I was trying to catch a frog, but he escaped and hid among some Brahmans. I bit a Brahman boy's toe by mistake, thinking it was a frog. The boy died, and his father cursed me to become a vehicle for frogs, relying on them for food."

The frog told all the other frogs about Slow-Poison's story. They were thrilled and informed the frog-king, Water-Foot. He and his counselors climbed onto Slow-Poison's hood, followed by the other frogs in order of age. Some frogs hopped behind the snake, and Slow-Poison showed off his skills.

Water-Foot was delighted with the ride and said, "I'd rather ride Slow-Poison than any other vehicle." The next day, Slow-Poison moved slowly, and Water-Foot asked, "Why don't you carry us as usual?" Slow-Poison replied, "I'm hungry, but I can eat the smaller frogs." Water-Footeven suggested that Slow-Poison should eat the plebeian frogs.

Slow-Poison was overjoyed and ate the frogs, growing strong in a few days. He thought to himself, "The trick worked. Now I have the power to eat all sorts of frogs." Water-Foot still trusted Slow-Poison.

Another black snake, a huge fellow, arrived and was shocked to see Slow-Poison carrying frogs. He said, "Partner, this is disgusting! They're our natural food." Slow-Poison explained that he was just following the Brahman's curse. He told the story again, pretending to be remorseful.

Moral: Sometimes, people take advantage of situations to get what they want, even if it means using others for their own benefit.

King Joy and Secretary Splendor

The kingdom of King Joy was renowned for its grandeur, with princes from far and wide paying homage to their ruler.

King Joy's secretary, Splendor, was a wise and learned man, but his wife often found fault with him. One day, she pouted and refused to speak to him.

Splendor begged his wife to tell him what was wrong and promised to fix it. His wife finally relented, saying that he must shave his head and fall at her feet to make amends.

Splendor did as he was told, and his wife forgave him. But King Joy's wife was not so easily placated. She refused to forgive him, no matter how many apologies he made.

In desperation, King Joy did something silly. He held a bridle in his mouth and let his wife ride on his back, making horse-like noises as he was led around the palace.

The next morning, Splendor appeared before the king, looking rather silly with his shaved head. The king asked him why he was in such a state, and Splendor explained that he had been forced to do it by his wife.

The king was amused and said, "It seems that you, too, are under your wife's thumb, just like Joy and I. You tried to find a way to get rid of your wife, but your own words betrayed you."

The king then told a story about a clever monkey who outwitted a crocodile. The monkey had seen the crocodile's sharp teeth and had decided to play a trick on him.

Moral: Silence is often the best policy, especially when dealing with someone who is being unreasonable.

The Dog Who Went Abroad

Spot, a dog from a town hit by a long famine, felt his throat constricted by hunger. He decided to leave his home and travel to another country in search of food.

In a new city, Spot found a careless housewife who left her food unattended. He entered her house every day and ate his fill from a variety of dishes. However, as he left, other dogs, fueled by arrogance, attacked him and tore him apart.

Spot realized that even in a foreign land, he faced danger and hardship. He thought, "It's better to return to my own city, where I can live peacefully, even during times of famine." So, he returned home.

When Spot's relatives asked him about his journey, he replied, "The food in the foreign land was delicious and varied. The people were easy-going, and the women were friendly. But the men were lacking in self-control."

Spot's story inspired the monkey to reflect on his own situation. He had been living with the crocodile, who had been forced to leave his home due to Spot's advice. But the monkey now realized that his carefree life was not worth the loss of his home.

The monkey decided to take action and defend his home against the desperate stranger who had taken it over. With courage and determination, the monkey fought back and killed the intruder, reclaiming his home.

Spot's journey taught him that it's always better to appreciate what you have, rather than seeking something new and potentially harmful.

The Four Treasure-Seekers

In a small town, four Brahmans lived as the best of friends. They were poor and struggled to make ends meet. One day, they had a heart-to-heart conversation about their situation. They decided that it was better to be dead than to live in poverty.

The Brahmans discussed various ways to make money, but they agreed that the only reliable method was through trade. They learned that trade had seven branches, including false weights and balances, price-boosting, and foreign trade. However, they also discovered that these methods were not always honest and could lead to trouble.

The Brahmans decided to try their luck in foreign trade. They traveled to the Avanti country, where they met a master-magician named Terror-Joy. He told them that he could give them magic quills that would lead them to treasure. The Brahmans were skeptical, but they decided to give it a try.

The magician gave each of them a magic quill and told them to go to the northern slope of the Himalaya Mountains. The quill would drop, and wherever it did, they would find treasure. The Brahmans followed the magician's instructions and soon found themselves in a beautiful but treacherous landscape.

As they journeyed on, the first quill dropped, revealing a treasure of copper. The Brahmans were overjoyed, but they soon realized that copper was not enough to solve their poverty problem. They decided to continue their search, and the second quill dropped, revealing a treasure of silver. Again, they were disappointed, thinking that gold must be ahead.

The third quill dropped, revealing a treasure of gold. The Brahmans were ecstatic, but they soon realized that gold was not the answer to their problems either. They decided to continue their search, and the fourth quill dropped, revealing a terrible sight: a man with a wheel whirling on his head.

The Brahmans were shocked and amazed. They asked the wheel-bearer how he had ended up in such a state, and he told them the story of how he had come to the place, just like them, and had been tortured by the wheel. The Brahmans realized that they had been foolish to think that treasure was the answer to their problems.

The gold-finder scolded his companion, saying, "I told you not to go any further. But you did not listen. Indeed, there is wisdom in the saying: 'Scholarship is less than sense; therefore seek intelligence.' You were blinded by your desire for treasure and did not use your common sense."

Moral: True wisdom and common sense are more valuable than wealth and material possessions.

The Unforgiving Monkey

In a certain city, King Moon had a pack of monkeys for his son's amusement. They were well-fed and happy.

One of the monkeys, a ram, had a habit of entering the kitchen and eating everything in sight. The cooks would beat him with sticks, but the chief monkey, wise and cautious, saw a bigger threat. "If the cooks get angry enough, they might use a firebrand, and the ram's woolly back will catch fire. The stable nearby is made of thatch, and if the ram burns, it will spread to the horses. And if the horses get burned, they'll need monkey-fat to heal. But we monkeys will be the ones to provide that fat, and we'll be the ones to die!"

The chief monkey gathered the other monkeys and warned them about the danger. "A quarrel between the ram and the cooks will mean our deaths. It's better for us to leave the palace and live in the forest."

But the monkeys laughed at the chief's warning. "You're old and your mind is slipping," they said. "We'll stay here and enjoy the good food the prince gives us."

The chief monkey sighed and left the palace, going to the forest to live. But he left behind a warning that would come too late.

One day, the ram entered the kitchen and the cooks, in a fit of rage, used a firebrand to beat him. The ram ran into the stable, causing a fire that burned the horses. The king was worried and asked his veterinary surgeons for a solution. They told him to use monkey-fat to heal the horses, but the king knew that meant the monkeys would have to die.

The king ordered the slaughter of the monkeys, and soon they were all dead. The chief monkey heard the news and was filled with sorrow.

As he wandered through the forest, he came across a lake with lotus flowers. He noticed that there were footprints leading into the lake, but none coming out. He realized that a monster must be living in the water, and he decided to drink from a lotus-stalk to avoid it.

But the monster, a man-eating fiend, saw the monkey and was impressed by his cleverness. The fiend asked the monkey what he wanted, and the monkey asked for the fiend's pearl necklace. The fiend agreed, and the monkey gave it to the king, telling him that he could get a similar necklace by bathing in a magical lake in the forest.

The king, greedy for more pearl necklaces, decided to go to the lake with his retinue. The monkey led them to the lake, and when they were all in the water, the fiend ate them. The king was the last one to be eaten, and as he was being swallowed, the monkey told him that he had planned this revenge for the death of his household.

Moral: Greed and a desire for revenge can lead to destruction and chaos.

Loss of Gains

Numskull and Red-Face were friends.

Numskull had a lot of fruit. He gave some to Red-Face.

Red-Face ate the fruit and said, "Thank you, Numskull."

Numskull gave Red-Face more fruit every day.

Red-Face ate and ate and got very fat.

He couldn't even walk. Numskull had to carry him.

Numskull said, "Red-Face, why did you eat so much?"

Red-Face said, "I was hungry and you gave me food."

Numskull said, "If you had worked for your food, you wouldn't be lazy now."

Red-Face said, "I'm sorry. I'll be careful next time."

But it was too late. Numskull had lost all his fruit.

Moral: Giving too much can lead to great loss.

Loss of Gains

In a forest, a monkey and a crocodile became friends.

The monkey, being very clever, thought of a plan to get the crocodile's wealth. He said, "My dear friend, I've heard that there's a great treasure hidden somewhere in the forest. Let's go find it together!" The crocodile, trusting the monkey, agreed to share the treasure equally.

As they searched, the monkey led the crocodile to a nearby river. The crocodile, eager to get to the treasure, jumped into the river. The monkey, however, didn't follow. He just called out, "I'll wait here while you dive deeper to find it!" The crocodile, blinded by greed, dived deeper into the river.

But when the crocodile came back up, he found that the monkey had taken all the treasure and run away. The crocodile realized too late that he had been tricked.

Moral: Greed and trusting strangers often lead to losing what you have.
